clue.text: Delius sets the tone for Powell's roman-fleuve?

definitions.text: Delius sets the tone for Powell's roman-fleuve?

parts.words: Delius sets the tone for Powell's roman-fleuve?
parts.note: a tone poem by the composer Delius whose title could stand as a motto for Anthony Powell's novel sequence A Dance to the Music of Time

explanation.surface: A composer's music is imagined as the overture to a long English novel sequence.
explanation.walkthrough: Delius wrote an orchestral piece of this name; Powell's twelve-novel roman-fleuve is A Dance to the Music of Time, so the Delius title sums up its theme.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of the Delius tone poem doubles as a fitting description of Powell's dance-themed cycle of novels.

clue.text: Way to recite in sort of poem?

parts.note: taken as written
a tone poem is an orchestral piece, so 'tone' names a sort of poem

explanation.surface: A question about how best to read a particular kind of verse aloud.
explanation.walkthrough: The scan's 'I' must be 'in': IN followed by TONE, as in tone poem, the orchestral form.
explanation.definitionFit: To intone is to chant or speak words in a level, measured voice, a way of reciting them.

clue.text: An often dotty literary omission

parts.note: a gap in a text marked by a row of dots, three full stops standing for missing words

explanation.surface: A slightly mad or scatterbrained thing left out of a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dotty' seems to mean eccentric, but here it means printed as dots.
explanation.definitionFit: The punctuation mark of three dots signals that words have been left out of a quoted passage.

clue.text: Novel and fantastic variations by Strauss

explanation.surface: A book and a piece of orchestral music by Richard Strauss.
explanation.walkthrough: Cervantes wrote the novel; Richard Strauss subtitled his tone poem of the same name 'fantastic variations on a theme of knightly character'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both the Cervantes novel about a deluded knight and the Strauss tone poem based on it bear this title.

clue.text: Most elegant as tenet, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps says the letters of the two words could be arranged some other way

explanation.surface: A doctrine described as the finest and most refined.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' signals rearranging AS TENET.
explanation.definitionFit: Neat means tidy and trim, so the superlative is the most elegant or smart.

clue.text: Kästner's young Berliner gives back fruit

indicators.note: gives back means the word for a citrus fruit is written in the opposite direction

parts.note: a lime is a green citrus fruit

explanation.surface: A boy from Berlin in a German children's book returns some fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gives back' turns LIME round. Erich Kästner wrote Emil and the Detectives, about a boy who goes to Berlin.
explanation.definitionFit: The hero of Kästner's children's novel Emil and the Detectives is a young boy in Berlin.

clue.text: Protagonist not Leander, anyway

parts.note: anti means against or opposed, a way of saying not
Leander, who swam the Hellespont nightly, is the hero of the legend, anyway

explanation.surface: A central character who is not like the romantic swimmer Leander.
explanation.walkthrough: Leander swam the Hellespont to his lover Hero; the clue plays on that name, since Leander is a hero of the story at any rate.
explanation.definitionFit: A central character lacking conventional heroic virtues is still the protagonist of the story.

clue.text: Titanic ballet

explanation.surface: A huge-scale dance piece.
explanation.walkthrough: Prometheus was a Titan, so he is Titanic in the literal sense; Beethoven wrote the ballet The Creatures of Prometheus.
explanation.definitionFit: The fire-stealing figure of myth was one of the Titans, and he gives his name to a Beethoven ballet score.

clue.text: Displaced weaver from Two Rivers

parts.note: the Marne is a river in northern France
R is the usual abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: A weaver who has left his home region by the meeting of two rivers.
explanation.walkthrough: Silas Marner, in George Eliot's novel, is a weaver driven from his town to the village of Raveloe.
explanation.definitionFit: George Eliot's Silas Marner is a linen weaver exiled from his community after a false accusation.

clue.text: Fast Greek girl picked up three golds

definitions.text: Fast Greek girl picked up three golds

parts.words: Fast Greek girl picked up three golds
parts.note: the swift huntress of Greek myth lost a footrace when she stopped for three golden apples rolled in her path

explanation.surface: A speedy Greek athlete collects three gold medals.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests Olympic medals; the golds are the golden apples Hippomenes dropped to slow her down.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek legend the fleet-footed runner was beaten in a race after stooping to gather golden apples.

clue.text: Time fell awkwardly in modest art form

indicators.note: awkwardly suggests the letters of the two words fall in a clumsy new order

explanation.surface: A moment of clumsiness within a humble kind of art.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awkwardly' rearranges TIME and FELL together.
explanation.definitionFit: A film made for television is a modest form of the cinema art, with smaller budget and audience.

clue.text: Good queen initiates better education system, say

indicators.note: initiates means the starting letters of the next words, those that begin each one

explanation.surface: A monarch starts a better school system.
explanation.walkthrough: Elizabeth I was known as Good Queen Bess.
explanation.definitionFit: Elizabeth I of England was popularly called Good Queen Bess, using a pet form of her name.

clue.text: Dramatist resisting bad actor

parts.note: bucking means resisting or opposing, as in bucking the trend
a ham is an actor who overplays

explanation.surface: A playwright stands up to a poor performer.
explanation.walkthrough: George Villiers, 2nd Duke of Buckingham, wrote the satirical play The Rehearsal.
explanation.definitionFit: The Restoration Duke of Buckingham was a playwright, author of the burlesque The Rehearsal.

clue.text: A small part of Dickens's opus

definitions.text: A small part of Dickens's opus

parts.words: A small part of Dickens's opus
parts.note: Dickens's novels first appeared serially, a monthly or weekly portion at a time

explanation.surface: A fragment of the novelist's output.
explanation.walkthrough: Dickens published his novels in monthly or weekly parts before they appeared as books.
explanation.definitionFit: Serial novels were issued piece by piece, each part one episode of the whole work.

clue.text: Conspirator, against David, finally suspended

parts.note: the Old Testament counsellor who joined Absalom's plot against King David and later hanged himself

explanation.surface: A plotter against David whose scheme was ultimately put on hold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suspended' seems to mean postponed, but in 2 Samuel the plotter hanged himself when his advice was ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Bible David's adviser defected to Absalom's rebellion and, when it failed, hanged himself.

clue.text: "I will in lodging lose this napkin" (Othello)

definitions.text: "I will in lodging lose this napkin" (Othello)

parts.words: "I will in lodging lose this napkin" (Othello)
parts.note: Iago's line in Othello names whose lodging he will plant the handkerchief in; the missing word is that lieutenant's name with a possessive

explanation.surface: A quotation from Othello with one word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: Iago says 'I will in Cassio's lodging lose this napkin', planting Desdemona's handkerchief on Othello's lieutenant.
explanation.definitionFit: Iago plans to leave the handkerchief in the rooms of Othello's lieutenant to fake evidence of adultery.

clue.text: Detached, like theatrical tables

explanation.surface: Stage furniture standing apart from one another.
explanation.walkthrough: Separate Tables is a pair of one-act plays by Terence Rattigan.
explanation.definitionFit: Separate means standing apart, and Rattigan's play Separate Tables puts the word into theatrical history.

clue.text: Burns's description of his wife might lose some, too

explanation.surface: Robert Burns praises his wife, who may also come off worse at times.
explanation.walkthrough: Burns wrote 'She is a winsome wee thing' about his wife Jean Armour; the proverb runs 'you win some, you lose some'.
explanation.definitionFit: Charming and attractive in Burns's song, and a person who wins some games may also lose some.

clue.text: He will be six foot two, / My / His haircut will be crew, / My "(Ira Gershwin)

definitions.text: He will be six foot two, / My / His haircut will be crew, / My "(Ira Gershwin)

parts.words: He will be six foot two, / My / His haircut will be crew, / My "(Ira Gershwin)
parts.note: a lyric by Ira Gershwin in which a parent imagines a daughter's future husband; the blank after each 'My' is that relation

explanation.surface: A song lyric imagining a tall young man with a crew cut.
explanation.walkthrough: The quoted lines leave a gap after 'My' that the solver fills with the family relation the lyric describes.
explanation.definitionFit: The parent singing pictures the man their daughter will marry, who becomes their relation by marriage.

clue.text: He's up to no good and by definition

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held 'He's up to no good and by definition' (7): 'He's up to no good' defines VILLAIN but 'and by definition' gives no letters or mechanism; likely garbled in OCR, and no source found.
annotationWithheld.clue: He's up to no good and by definition

clue.text: Homer's VIP I somehow leave the poorer

indicators.note: somehow says the letters of these words are to be put together in some other order

explanation.surface: A great epic poet's important person is somehow made poorer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somehow' rearranges HOMERS VIP I, the apostrophe ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: To make someone poorer is to reduce them to poverty.

clue.text: John Podsnap sagely included these restorative pauses

indicators.note: included says the letters sit inside the run of words before it

explanation.surface: Dickens's pompous Mr Podsnap wisely took short rests.
explanation.walkthrough: Podsnap is the complacent gentleman in Dickens's Our Mutual Friend.
explanation.definitionFit: Short sleeps taken in the day restore energy, little pauses from activity.

clue.text: Mr Snevellici, for example, rose up with difficulty

indicators.note: with difficulty suggests the two words are wrenched into another order

explanation.surface: A Dickens actor gets to his feet with an effort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with difficulty' rearranges ROSE UP. Mr Snevellici is a showy actor in Dickens's Nicholas Nickleby.
explanation.definitionFit: The theatrical Mr Snevellici of Nicholas Nickleby is an affected show-off, posing for effect.

clue.text: Embryonic work of Zola

explanation.surface: An early novel by Émile Zola.
explanation.walkthrough: Germinal is Zola's novel of a miners' strike.
explanation.definitionFit: Germinal describes something in its earliest stage of growth, and it is also the title of Zola's mining novel.

clue.text: Returning professor has point, gets signs of approval

indicators.note: Returning means the word for a university teacher is read backwards

parts.note: a don is a university teacher
S, south, is a compass point

explanation.surface: A professor comes back with a point and is met with approval.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Returning' turns DON into NOD.
explanation.definitionFit: Bobbing the head up and down shows agreement, so these movements are signs of assent.

clue.text: A cold English Saturday suggesting a victim of Paris

parts.note: a chill is a cold, with the article kept
S is the abbreviation for Saturday

explanation.surface: A chilly English weekend day that hints at a mythical victim.
explanation.walkthrough: Paris here is the Trojan prince, whose arrow killed the Greek hero at Troy, not the French capital.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek legend the Trojan prince shot the Greek champion in his vulnerable heel.

clue.text: "Services are voluntary: that is to say you must either ( all or none" Waugh. waugh)

definitions.text: "Services are voluntary: that is to say you must either ( all or none" Waugh. waugh)

parts.words: "Services are voluntary: that is to say you must either ( all or none" Waugh. waugh)
parts.note: a line from Evelyn Waugh with a blank where the verb for going to the services belongs

explanation.surface: A quotation from Waugh about compulsory chapel dressed up as voluntary.
explanation.walkthrough: The Waugh quotation leaves out the verb: you must go to all the services or none.
explanation.definitionFit: To go to or be present at a church service is the verb missing from the quotation.

clue.text: Some of Vincent bloomers which proved very costly

definitions.text: Some of Vincent bloomers which proved very costly

parts.words: Some of Vincent bloomers which proved very costly
parts.note: Van Gogh's paintings of yellow flowers, one of which sold at auction for a record price

explanation.surface: A painter's mistakes that turned out to be expensive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloomers' looks like blunders, but they are flowers; one of Van Gogh's paintings of them fetched a record price in 1987.
explanation.definitionFit: Van Gogh painted a celebrated series of vases of these tall yellow flowers, now worth fortunes.
